messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane is a 63-year-old married man of Māori background who has worked for many years as a financial analyst, a job that once suited his patience, concentration, and preference for orderly routines. He describes his life as having divided sharply after a night-time car accident that he experienced as unmistakably life-threatening. He had been driving home in the dark when another vehicle came fast into his path. What has stayed with him most vividly is not a tidy sequence but fragments that still arrive with the force of the original moment: the sudden sound of cars around him, the enclosed darkness beyond the windshield, and a sharp smell from the crash scene that he can still identify in an instant before he has time to tell himself where he is. Even now, when he speaks about it, he does so as if some parts are not properly filed away in the past. He says that certain moments do not feel remembered so much as re-entered.

In the weeks after the accident, Tane tried to return to normal by going back to work and keeping family life steady with his wife. Outwardly, he resumed many responsibilities, but he found himself moving through the world as if danger were close by and likely to return without warning. He came to believe that he had to be on guard all the time. Entering any room, whether it was a conference space at the office, a restaurant, or even a medical waiting room, he found himself automatically scanning for exits before he could settle into whatever he was there to do. He did not describe this as a choice so much as something his body insisted on. He often says that his body reacts before his mind has even caught up, as if some part of him has already detected a threat.

That sense of instant alarm is most obvious around the triggers that now structure much of his day. In the parking garage beneath his office building, the dimness and enclosed dark spaces can make his chest tighten before he reaches the elevator. The sound of cars outside the building, especially when engines rev suddenly or tires pass close to the curb, can pull him out of spreadsheets and meetings and place him back in the accident so abruptly that for a moment it feels as though it is happening right now. At times, when this occurs, he hears in his head the sounds from that night with an almost immediate clarity. He is not merely thinking about the crash; he is listening to it again. Certain related smells are especially potent. If he catches them unexpectedly, whether near traffic, in a garage, or around a roadside stop, the full memory can come back without warning, vivid and complete enough that he has to stop and orient himself.

Over time, Tane has organized his life around the possibility of being caught off guard. He is certain that constant vigilance is necessary because you never know what can happen next. At night he often wakes and checks whether he is safe before he can settle again. His wife has noticed him listening intently in the dark, sometimes getting out of bed to check the house, not because he has heard anything definite but because he feels he cannot simply assume safety. During the day he tries hard not to let his mind dwell on the accident. He has come to believe that if he thinks about it directly, he will not be able to handle what follows. Because of that, he cuts off conversations, changes the subject when his wife asks how he is doing, and throws himself into numerical work when he senses the memory approaching.

These habits have gradually narrowed his world. At work, he prefers rooms where he can sit near the door and becomes tense in longer meetings held in windowless conference rooms. He times his arrival and departure to avoid lingering in the darker parts of the garage, and he is more distracted by traffic sounds than he used to be. At home, his wife experiences him as present but guarded, as though part of him is always monitoring something just beyond the moment they are sharing. Tane sought help only after recognizing that this stance had not eased with time. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of nights spent waking to check for safety, days interrupted by sudden sensory reminders, and the growing sense that he was living braced against the next disaster. He says he wants relief, but what frightens him most is the possibility that if he lets his guard down or allows himself to think fully about the accident, he will lose control of something he has spent years trying to contain.
